Psychiatric Emergencies & Crisis

Psychiatric emergencies — suicide, violence, catatonia, serotonin syndrome, NMS and crisis intervention.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Recognise common psychiatric emergencies
  • Manage violence and suicidal patients safely
  • Describe crisis intervention
  • Explain emergency medicines and restraints

In simple words

A psychiatric emergency needs immediate action to protect life and safety. The first priorities are always safety, airway, breathing and circulation, then the mental state.

Common psychiatric emergencies

  • Suicide attempt — poisoning, hanging, cutting
  • Violence and rage — may be due to psychosis, intoxication or withdrawal
  • Catatonia — mutism, rigidity, refusal of food and water
  • Neuroleptic malignant syndrome — fever, rigidity, altered mind
  • Serotonin syndrome — shivering, diarrhoea, clonus, high fever
  • Severe drug withdrawal — alcohol, benzodiazepines
  • Puerperal psychosis — restlessness, refusal to feed the baby, delusions

Crisis intervention steps

  1. Ensure safety — of the patient, staff and others
  2. Assess — level of risk, cause, supports
  3. Listen actively — let the person talk about what happened
  4. Stabilise — find safe strategies, involve family
  5. Plan — concrete steps, resources and follow-up
  6. Follow up and evaluate

🔴 Suicide precautions

Do not leave the patient alone, do not promise secrecy, and do not allow access to means. Medicines, sharp objects, ropes, belts and windows are risks. One-to-one observation, remove means and regular documentation are mandatory.

Where the nurse uses this

  • Emergency room — manage overdose, violence and self-harm
  • Ward — observation rounds, restraint checks, prevent suicide methods
  • Perinatal unit — screen and protect mothers with postpartum psychosis
  • Crisis situations — family disputes, grief, disaster and accidents

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Safety comes first in every psychiatric emergency.
  2. Suicide: ask directly, remove means, constant observation, no secrecy.
  3. Violence: keep two nurse lengths distance, escape routes, calm speech.
  4. Catatonia needs feeding, hydration, physiotherapy and ECT.
  5. NMS = fever + rigidity + altered mind; a medical emergency.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Suicide risk rises after discharge from hospital.
  2. Self-harm is common in borderline personality disorder.
  3. Rapid-acting medicines like IM haloperidol may be prescribed for acute agitation.
  4. Restraint is the last resort with continuous monitoring and regular release.
  5. Naloxone reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression.

📌 Memory trick

Suicide safety: S-A-R — Supervise, Ask, Remove the means.

60-second revision

  • Emergencies: suicide, violence, catatonia, NMS, serotonin syndrome, withdrawal.
  • First step in any emergency is safety.
  • Suicidal patients are never left alone, and means are removed.
  • Violence de-escalation: calm, distance, space, escort.
  • Restraints only as last resort with monitoring and release checks.

Test yourself

The first step in managing a violent patient is:

Answer: B. Safety of everyone comes first; verbal de-escalation and a clear escape route reduce danger.

A suicidal patient is managed by:

Answer: B. Suicidal patients need continuous observation and removal of every means of self-harm.

Catatonia in schizophrenia may be treated with:

Answer: B. ECT can be life-saving in malignant catatonia and refusal of food and fluids.

Fever with severe muscular rigidity on antipsychotics is:

Answer: B. NMS presents with fever, severe rigidity, sweating and altered mind; stop the drug immediately.

Restraints should be used:

Answer: B. Restraints are a last resort, documented and reviewed regularly with circulation checks.
